title: Off-Grid Solar System Size Calculator | Wattlyst
meta: Plan a full off-grid solar system: panels, battery bank, inverter and charge controller from your appliance list and backup days.
primary_keyword: off grid solar system size calculator
author: ali-ahmad

sections.h2: How is an off-grid solar system designed?
p: Off-grid means no grid at all: the panels make every unit, the battery carries every night and the inverter runs every appliance. So each part is sized from the appliance list. The panels must make the day's 5.9 units, refill what the battery gave at night with its charging and inverter losses (6.6 units in all), and carry the 1,141 W running load at noon; the larger rule gives 1.66 kW, or 3 panels of 585 W. The battery must hold the load after sunset: 1,141 W for 4 hours is 4.6 units, which at 48 V with lithium is 118 Ah. The inverter must carry 1,141 W with a margin and accept the panels: 1.43 kW, with a surge of 2,341 W for the pump motor.
Everything in the list counts, including the appliances that run for minutes, because there is no grid to fall back on. Check each one's watts against its label before trusting the result.

sections.h2: Off-grid battery bank size and days of autonomy
p: This calculator sizes the battery for one night: the full running load for the hours you enter. That is honest about what it covers and what it does not. It assumes every listed appliance runs together for those hours, which is a worst case for the evening, but it does not add a second cloudy day. For 4 hours the bank is 118 Ah (5.6 kWh) at 48 V; for the whole 12 hour night it is 353 Ah (16.9 kWh).

Off-grid homes usually plan for two days of autonomy, three where winter fog or monsoon clouds last for days. Take the night units from this result to the solar battery size calculator, enter the days of autonomy, and the bank grows in proportion. The panels then also have to refill a larger bank on the first sunny day, so add panels beyond the figure here; this page adds the charging losses for one night, not the catch-up after a cloudy spell.

The inverter is sized mainly from the running watts of everything that can be on at once: 1,141 W × 1.25 = 1.43 kW. It must also accept the panels: inverters take an array up to about 1.3 times their rating, so it is never smaller than 1.76 kW ÷ 1.3 = 1.35 kW. The larger gives a 1.43 kW off-grid or hybrid inverter. Its surge rating must cover the largest motor start, here 2,341 W for the water pump; a non-inverter fridge or AC pushes that figure up fast.
Buy an inverter whose battery voltage matches the bank you chose and whose MPPT input can take the panel kW and string voltage; the charge controller size calculator explains those limits.

sections.h2: Off-grid solar for a home with an AC
p: Add a 1 ton inverter AC for eight hours and the daily energy nearly doubles to 11.1 units, the running load rises to 2,041 W, and the system becomes 6 panels (3.51 kW), a 210 Ah bank at 48 V (10.1 kWh) and a 2.7 kW inverter. The AC in the evening is what makes off-grid expensive; running it only in daylight keeps the battery small.

sections.h2: Off-grid solar kit size for a cabin or shop
p: A cabin with four LED bulbs, two DC fans, a small TV and phone charging uses only 1.4 units a day at 188 W, so one 585 W panel, a 39 Ah lithium bank at 24 V and a 0.45 kW inverter cover it. DC fans and LED lights are the cheapest way to shrink an off-grid system, because every watt saved at night comes off the battery.

faq.q: How do I size an off-grid solar system?
faq.a: From the appliance list: panels from the daily units, the battery refill and the midday load (3 panels, 1.76 kW for the house above), a battery from the load after sunset (118 Ah at 48 V for 4 hours), and an inverter from the running watts, at least the panels ÷ 1.3 (1.43 kW).

faq.q: How big should the off-grid battery bank be?
faq.a: Enough for the load after sunset times the hours it runs, divided by the bank volts, the usable share and the inverter efficiency: 118 Ah at 48 V for 4 hours here, 353 Ah for a full 12 hour night. Add days of autonomy for cloudy weather in the solar battery size calculator.

faq.q: What size inverter for an off-grid system?
faq.a: The running watts of everything on at once times the 1.25 margin, but never less than the panel kW ÷ 1.3, because an inverter accepts only so much array: 1.43 kW for the house above, with a surge rating of at least 2,341 W for the pump. The battery does not set the inverter size.

faq.q: Can an off-grid solar system run an AC?
faq.a: Yes, if it is sized for it. One 1 ton inverter AC for eight hours takes the small house to 6 panels and a 210 Ah bank at 48 V with a 2.7 kW inverter. Running it in daylight only keeps the battery far smaller.

faq.q: Lithium or tubular for an off-grid home?
faq.a: Lithium: the same night needs 5.6 kWh of lithium but 10.1 kWh of tubular, and lithium takes a daily deep cycle for many more years. Tubular only wins on purchase price.

faq.q: Why is the battery bigger than the house uses in a day?
faq.a: The twelve-hour worst case assumes every appliance runs all night, which is more than the daily total. Enter the hours the full load really runs after sunset, usually about four, and keep the rest of the night for the fridge and a fan.

faq.q: Do I need a charge controller for an off-grid system?
faq.a: Yes, either built into a hybrid or off-grid inverter or as a separate MPPT. Its amps come from the panel watts and the bank voltage; the charge controller size calculator gives the size.

key_facts: An off-grid solar system has three parts sized separately: panels from the daily units plus the battery refill (6.6 units ÷ 4 per kW in Lahore = 1.66 kW), a battery from the load after sunset (118 Ah at 48 V for 4 hours), and an inverter from the running watts (1,141 W × 1.25 = 1.43 kW), never smaller than the panels ÷ 1.3 (1.35 kW); here 1.43 kW.
The battery bank for one night is sized for the full running load for the hours you enter; running it for the whole 12 hour night needs 353 Ah at 48 V (16.9 kWh), against 118 Ah for 4 hours.
A tubular bank for the same night is 423 Ah at 24 V (10.1 kWh) because only 50% of it may be used, against 90% for lithium.
Adding one 1 ton inverter AC for eight hours takes the same house to 11.1 units a day, 6 panels (3.51 kW), a 210 Ah bank at 48 V and a 2.7 kW inverter.

Off-grid panels are sized here on the yearly average sun, so in January, the weakest month for the city picked, they make about 5.2 units a day against 6.6 needed (22% short in that month, 4 months short in the year); a generator or a lighter load covers those months.
mistakes: Sizing the panels for the day only. Off-grid, the panels must also put back what the battery gave at night, plus charging and inverter losses; this calculator adds them, a simple daily-units rule does not.
Planning one night of battery for an off-grid house. Two cloudy days in a row empty a one-night bank; use the solar battery size calculator with days of autonomy.
Running the AC on the battery. One inverter AC in the evening more than doubles the bank; run it in daylight or plan the battery for it.
Forgetting the pump's surge. The inverter must start the motor; its surge rating must cover 2,341 W here, not just the running load.
Using tubular batteries to 90%. Only about 50% of a tubular bank may be used nightly; the calculator already allows for the type you pick.

how.tpl: Energy: watts × quantity × hours a day for every appliance = {{out.daily_kwh|1}} units a day; the night share, {{out.night_kwh|1}} units, comes from the battery, so the panels must refill it through charging and inverter losses: {{out.day_kwh|1}} + {{out.night_kwh|1}} ÷ ({{out.battery_inverter_eff|pct}} × {{out.charge_eff|pct}}) = {{out.array_kwh|1}} units a day, ÷ {{out.yield_kwh_per_kwp_day|1}} units per kW of panels a day in your city = {{out.kw_energy|2}} kW. Power: the panels must also carry the {{out.running_w|int}} W running load at midday, ÷ {{out.pr|2}} performance ratio = {{out.kw_power|2}} kW. The larger, {{out.kw|2}} kW, rounded up to whole {{out.panel_w}} W panels = {{out.panels|int}} panels, {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW. Battery: {{out.running_w|int}} W × {{out.night_hours}} hours = {{out.night_kwh|1}} units after sunset, ÷ ({{out.battery_v}} V × {{out.battery_dod|pct}} usable × inverter efficiency) = {{out.battery_ah|up}} Ah, a bank of {{out.battery_kwh|1}} kWh. Inverter: the larger of {{out.running_w|int}} W × {{out.margin|2}} = {{out.inverter_kw_load|2}} kW for the load and {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW of panels ÷ {{out.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} = {{out.inverter_kw_array|2}} kW, so the panels are never more than {{out.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} times the inverter: {{out.inverter_kw|up2}} kW continuous (the size to buy: {{out.inverter_buy}}), with a surge rating of at least {{out.inverter_surge_w|int}} W for the pump. Weakest month: in {{out.worst_month|raw}} the same panels make about {{out.worst_month_kwh|1}} units a day against the {{out.array_kwh|1}} needed, {{out.worst_short_pct|int}}% short; the size above is set on the yearly average sun, so plan a generator, fewer loads or more panels for any month that comes up short.
how.text: Energy: watts × quantity × hours a day for every appliance = 5.9 units a day; the night share, 4.6 units, comes from the battery, so the panels must refill it through charging and inverter losses: 1.3 + 4.6 ÷ (90% × 95%) = 6.6 units a day, ÷ 4 units per kW of panels a day in your city = 1.66 kW. Power: the panels must also carry the 1,141 W running load at midday, ÷ 0.78 performance ratio = 1.46 kW. The larger, 1.66 kW, rounded up to whole 585 W panels = 3 panels, 1.76 kW. Battery: 1,141 W × 4 hours = 4.6 units after sunset, ÷ (48 V × 90% usable × inverter efficiency) = 118 Ah, a bank of 5.6 kWh. Inverter: the larger of 1,141 W × 1.25 = 1.43 kW for the load and 1.76 kW of panels ÷ 1.3 = 1.35 kW, so the panels are never more than 1.3 times the inverter: 1.43 kW continuous (the size to buy: 1.5 kW), with a surge rating of at least 2,341 W for the pump. Weakest month: in January the same panels make about 5.2 units a day against the 6.6 needed, 22% short; the size above is set on the yearly average sun, so plan a generator, fewer loads or more panels for any month that comes up short.

msg.drive_above_standard_sizes: This drive is above the largest size we list. Use one larger solar pump drive rated for this motor (two drives cannot share one motor) and ask the supplier or a licensed engineer; the size shown is the calculated minimum.
msg.motor_v_invalid: Pick the motor voltage from the list: 220 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase.
msg.string_below_bus: The panels in series are capped by the drive's maximum DC input on a cold morning, so on hot afternoons the string gives less than the voltage the motor needs at full speed and the pump runs slower then (see the string voltage in the working). Check the drive's DC input range with the supplier.
msg.above_standard_sizes: This is above the largest standard size we list. Split the array or circuit into two, or ask a licensed electrician or engineer; the sizes shown are the calculated minimums.
msg.generator_above_standard_sizes: This is above the largest generator size we list. Use two generators on separate circuits or a larger industrial set, and ask a licensed electrician; the size shown is the calculated minimum.

msg.usage_both: Both boxes are filled, so the units a day are used and the monthly units are left out. Clear the daily box to size from your bill.

content.answer: A small off-grid house with three fans, eight LED bulbs, an inverter fridge, a TV, a pump and a router needs 1.76 kW of panels (3 panels), a 118 Ah lithium bank at 48 V for 4 hours of the full load after sunset, and a 1.43 kW inverter. Panels = (day units + night units ÷ charging and inverter efficiency) ÷ sun yield; battery = night units ÷ (volts × usable share × efficiency).

formula.text: kW = max(E_day ÷ yield, P_run ÷ 1000 ÷ PR); panels = ceil(kW × 1000 ÷ W_panel); Ah = P_run × h_night ÷ (V × DoD × η); P_inv = max(P_run × m, kW × 1000 ÷ r_max)
lines: E_day = Σ watts × qty × hours ÷ 1000, units used in a full day
yield = units one kW of panels makes a day in your city
P_run = total running watts; PR = performance ratio
h_night = hours the full load runs from the battery after sunset
V = bank voltage; DoD = usable share of the battery; η = inverter efficiency
m = inverter margin; r_max = largest panel-to-inverter (DC/AC) ratio; surge ≥ largest starting load

content.safety: An off-grid system has no grid breaker to protect it; the DC fuses, isolators, earthing and the battery wiring must be installed by a licensed electrician or a certified solar installer, and the inverter must never be fed from both the battery and a generator without a proper changeover.
